sections.h2: Who sets and collects property tax
sections.html:
The state sets the value, and your county or town turns it into a bill. SDAT assesses real property and certifies the assessments to counties and municipalities, and those governments apply their own rates.

The system covers more than 2.3 million real property accounts across 23 counties, Baltimore City and 155 incorporated municipalities. Each state, county and municipal government sets its own rate, and the state doesn't cap rates. When a proposed rate is higher than the current one, the governing body must advertise it and hold a public hearing.

Two bills can land on one address: a county bill and a town or city bill. Ask the title company to confirm both are paid at closing.

The State's real property rate is $0.112 per $100 of assessed value, and county rates differ widely on top of it. In the FY 2022-23 rate sheet, Baltimore City was highest at 2.2480 per $100, followed by Baltimore County at 1.1000, Frederick at 1.0600, Garrett at 1.0560 and Howard at 1.0140. Prince George's was 1.0000 and Anne Arundel 0.9330, with Wicomico at 0.9070 and Worcester at 0.8450. Montgomery was lowest of those at 0.6940.

Those county figures are a snapshot, so ask the county for the current year's rate. A bill equals the assessment times the jurisdiction's rate, so a house in Baltimore City and an identical one in Montgomery County can carry very different taxes. Municipal governments set their own rates as well.

Every property is reassessed once every three years. Each county is split into three regions, so about one-third of its accounts are reviewed each year. Owners hear about a change in late December, when SDAT mails an assessment notice showing old and new market values with an appeal form.

Increases are phased in evenly over three years. A value rising from $100,000 to $130,000 is taxed at $110,000, then $120,000, then $130,000. A decrease takes effect right away.

The 2026 cycle covered Group 2 and brought a 12.7% overall increase in assessed value, with residential up an average of 13.2% and commercial up 11%. That compares with 20.1% in the 2025 cycle and 23.4% in 2023. Those are statewide averages, so your own notice is the number that counts.

Payment is due July 1, and no interest accrues through September 30. Past that date the account is in arrears under Tax-Property § 10-102.

  • Bills go out each July or August for the fiscal year that starts July 1.
  • Counties and municipalities must offer a semiannual schedule for owner-occupied principal residences. The first installment is due July 1 and payable without interest through September 30, and the second is due December 1 and payable without interest through December 31.
  • The second installment can be prepaid through September 30 with no service charge.
  • Otherwise a service charge of no more than 1.5% of the second installment applies, plus capped administrative costs.

Interest after the overdue date is set locally. It runs 1% per month in Anne Arundel County and 1.5% per month in Allegany County, so call your own county's collector for the current rule.

You start with the local assessment office, and you have 45 days from the date on the notice. The appeal can go through four levels, each with its own clock.

LevelDeadlineWho decides
Supervisor's level45 days from the notice dateAn assessor designated by the Supervisor of Assessments
Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board30 days from the final noticeLocal residents appointed by the Governor
Maryland Tax Court30 days from the board's orderAn independent body, in-person hearing
Circuit CourtFurther appealReviews the record for legal error

There is no filing fee at the board or Tax Court. SDAT tries to finish reassessment appeals by June 1, and the Supervisor's hearing is informal and usually about 15 minutes.

sections.h2: What evidence helps in an appeal?
sections.html:
Market-value evidence carries weight at a hearing. Complaints about the size of the bill carry none. Explain why the Total New Market Value doesn't reflect market value, point out errors on the property worksheet such as a wrong bathroom or fireplace count, and bring comparable sales.

Leave out past values, percentage increases, metropolitan cost arguments, tax bill amounts, and services received or not received. At the Tax Court, any outside properties you plan to cite must be listed at least 10 days in advance with sale date and price or assessment details.

Buyers have a separate path. If a property transfers between January 1 and June 30, the new owner can file a Petition for Review within 60 days of the transfer, once the deed is recorded in the land records. Owners can also file a petition for review by the first working day after January 1 in the two years when the property isn't being reassessed, if they believe value has fallen.

The main programs are the Homestead Tax Credit, the income-based Homeowners' Tax Credit and a deferral for older owners.

  • Homestead Tax Credit: applies when a principal residence's taxable assessment rises more than the local cap, which is 10% or lower. One application establishes eligibility.
  • Homeowners' Tax Credit: an income-based sliding scale that has delivered over $58 million in credits, with a $60,000 household income ceiling.
  • Property tax deferral: open to owners 65 or older where the local government has adopted it. The deferred amount becomes a lien and is repaid on transfer.

Religious, charitable and educational organizations may be exempt on property they own and use, and so may government property.

sections.h2: What happens if property tax goes unpaid?
sections.html:
The county can sell the tax lien at public auction, but the homeowner stays the owner. The buyer receives a tax lien certificate and may later ask a court to foreclose the right of redemption.

At least 30 days before the first advertisement, the Collector mails the owner of record a notice of the taxes owed. The sale is then advertised weekly for four successive weeks. A buyer can file a foreclosure case no earlier than six months after the sale, or nine months for owner-occupied homes under state law and in Baltimore City, and must file within two years of the certificate date or it becomes void.

The owner can redeem until the court forecloses, by paying the sale price, interest, later taxes and penalties in certified funds. If redemption happens more than four months after the sale, the owner also reimburses the certificate holder's expenses and attorney's fees. The State Tax Sale Ombudsman can be reached at (833) 732-8411.

Unpaid property tax is a lien, and a tax sale starts from that lien. Some counties also include water, sewer or special charges in it.

If you're behind, ask the county for the exact payoff and the sale date. A payoff letter goes to the title company so the lien is paid from your proceeds at closing. If a tax sale has already happened, ask the Ombudsman or the county for the redemption figure and the deadline. Costs rise the longer the lien sits, so the earlier you call, the smaller the number. A cash buyer can close on a short timeline, which helps when the clock on redemption is running.

faqs.q: When are Maryland property taxes due?
faqs.a: They are due July 1 and can be paid without interest through September 30. Owner-occupied homes can use a semiannual plan, with the second installment due December 1.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Maryland assessment?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the date on the assessment notice. The next appeal goes to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days of the final notice.

faqs.q: How often does Maryland reassess property?
faqs.a: Every three years. Increases are phased in evenly over three years, and decreases take effect immediately.

faqs.q: Do I lose my house if I miss a property tax payment?
faqs.a: Not right away. The county sells the tax lien, and the owner keeps the property and can redeem it until a court forecloses the right of redemption.

faqs.q: Can a buyer appeal an assessment after purchase?
faqs.a: Yes, for a transfer between January 1 and June 30. The buyer files a Petition for Review within 60 days of the transfer, after the deed is recorded.
